slides.say: Triangle A B C is a right triangle. Given: angle A B C is ninety degrees, A B is seven centimeters, and A C is ten centimeters. What is B C, in centimeters?

Again a right triangle with the right angle at B. But this time we know a leg and the hypotenuse, and we need the other leg. A C is across from the right angle, so A C, ten, is the hypotenuse, and B C is a leg.
at: so A C, ten, is the hypotenuse

slides.say: [short pause] The theorem is still the same: A B squared plus B C squared equals A C squared. We need B C squared, so we subtract A B squared from both sides. That leaves B C squared equals A C squared minus A B squared, the hypotenuse squared minus the other leg squared.
at: The theorem is still the same

slides.say: Ten squared is a hundred, and seven squared is forty-nine. A hundred minus forty-nine is fifty-one. So B C squared is fifty-one. Fifty-one isn't a perfect square, because seven squared is forty-nine and eight squared is sixty-four. So, like last time, we use the square root, and B C is the square root of fifty-one. Choice number four is our answer.
at: and B C is the square root
Choice number four is our answer

slides.say: Careful, three is ten minus seven. We subtract the squares, not the lengths. And the root of a hundred forty-nine adds the squares, as if B C were the hypotenuse. But B C is a leg, so it must be shorter than ten.
at: Careful, three is ten minus seven
And the root of a hundred forty-nine

slides.say: This is the base of the Pythagorean theorem. When two sides of a right triangle are known, we can always find the third. For the hypotenuse, we add the squares. For a leg, we subtract. Either way, that gives the side squared, so at the end we take the square root. It's a technique you really must master.

slides: Soon we'll learn shortcuts for it, Pythagorean triples and special right triangles. And there's a short lesson that proves the theorem. You don't have to watch it, but I warmly recommend it. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next question.
